Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I should have protected others and I failed

vignette: John, a 61-year-old North American male and bus driver, has been struggling with significant psychological distress following his traumatic experience of torture. His symptoms have progressively worsened over time, leading him to seek help now. The event that continues to haunt John occurred several months ago when he was abducted by individuals who subjected him to relentless physical and emotional torment. The intensity and brutality of the torture left lasting scars on both his body and mind. Since then, John has found it increasingly difficult to feel safe at night, as his senses remain heightened and vigilant for any signs of danger. John's nightly vigilance is a direct result of his negative appraisals, which are deeply entrenched in his belief that he should have done more to protect himself and others during the ordeal. This constant feeling of guilt and weakness amplifies his sense of vulnerability at night. He often lies awake listening for any unusual sounds, convinced that someone might be trying to break into his home again. The memory of the torture is a recurring nightmare for John. Each time he recalls specific details, it brings back the same terror he felt during the actual event. Certain moments are crystal clear in his mind, while others remain hazy and incomplete. These partial recollections make him feel like he is only remembering parts of what happened, leaving gaps that he cannot fill. This fragmented memory exacerbates his sense of threat, as it makes him constantly worry about missing details that could have prevented the torture. Moreover, John's negative appraisals are further reinforced by these incomplete and terrifying memories. He believes he should have been able to protect himself better and feels a profound sense of failure for not doing so. This belief in his own weakness has left him feeling powerless and constantly on edge, as if he is always one step away from another traumatic event. John's occupation as a bus driver presents its own set of challenges. The sounds and movements associated with driving often trigger physical reactions that remind him of the torture. He finds himself reacting to sudden noises or unexpected movements in ways that disrupt his ability to focus on driving safely. This has led to increased anxiety and self-doubt, further intensifying his negative appraisals. The combination of these factors has created a cycle of increasing distress for John. His fear and vigilance at night are compounded by the terror brought back through fragmented memories, which in turn reinforce his negative beliefs about himself. These beliefs then heighten his sense of threat, leading to even more intense vigilance and fear. What finally brought John to seek help was the realization that he could no longer manage these overwhelming feelings on his own. He is most afraid of losing control completely and failing to protect others again. Despite this fear, he hopes for a way to regain some semblance of normalcy in his life and to find peace with his past. John’s journey into therapy marks an important step towards addressing the deeply rooted cognitive and emotional challenges that have been plaguing him since the traumatic event. Through understanding and gradually working through these interconnected issues, John aims to break free from the cycle of fear and self-doubt that has dominated his life.
